text.p: A 12-day drivers' strike disrupting public transport in French cities weakened its grip on Monday after police cleared pickets in Toulouse and employers made concessions to drivers' demands for shorter hours.

In Toulouse, a bastion of the stoppages which began 22 days ago in the south-western city, police cleared about 100 pickets blocking a bus depot shortly after dawn to let about 30 percent of buses run.

In the northern city of Lille, a majority of striking bus and tram drivers voted to return to work following an agreement to cut the working week from 38 hours to 35 without reducing pay and to grant them an extra two weeks' annual holiday.

Other strikes, which started 12 days ago and have disrupted buses, trams and underground Metro trains in about 20 provincial cities, were still affecting Nice, Cannes, Clermont-Ferrand, Sete, Toulon and Le Mans.

Unions are divided over whether to recommend a return to work after management late last week met some of their central demands -- for a shorter working week with no pay cut, and retirement at 55 rather than at 60.
Transport resumed in Perpignan on Saturday.
In Toulouse, where buses have been running sporadically since a court on Saturday ordered fines for any drivers blocking traffic, non-strikers operated about 50 buses on Monday.
The strikes are the latest labour challenge to the centre-right government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, which last year bowed to truckers' demands for retirement at 55 after they blocked roads.
But it has said that state pension funds would be bankrupted if all workers were allowed to retire at 55.
